title: Design a Multi Tool AI Agent Using MCP

blocks.text: A multi tool AI agent is not just one model with a lot of context stuffed in. It is an orchestrator that decides which tool to call, when, and under what permissions.
This interview question tests whether you can turn a vague product idea into a clean map of servers, native functions, and guardrails.
We will walk through a repeatable framework for this, then apply it fully to a concrete customer support agent.
1. Clarify What the Agent Needs to Accomplish

blocks.alt: Clarify What the Agent Needs to Accomplish
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590831-501370521.png
Before naming a single tool, get clear on what job the agent is doing for the user and for the business.
Ask which systems already hold the data or perform the actions the agent needs, a CRM, a ticketing tool, an email provider.

items: Who is the end user, a customer, an internal employee, or another automated system?
What actions does the agent need to take, or is it read only for now?
Which existing systems of record does it need to touch?
What happens today without this agent, and what does success look like?
What is truly out of scope, so you do not over design the first version?

blocks.text: 2. Map Capabilities to MCP Servers or Native Functions
Not every capability needs to be an MCP server. Some logic belongs inside the agent process as a plain function call.
MCP servers earn their place when a capability talks to an external system and could be reused by another agent or client later.
Native functions fit purely internal logic, formatting a date, scoring sentiment, or summarizing a long tool result before it goes back to the model.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Capability","MCP Server or Native","Why"],"rows":[["Look up an order by id","MCP server","Talks to an external order system, reusable by other tools"],["Search a knowledge base","MCP server","Wraps a real search index other agents could also query"],["Send an email reply","MCP server","Talks to an external email provider with real side effects"],["Format a currency amount","Native function","Pure logic, no external system, no reuse benefit worth the overhead"],["Score message urgency","Native function","Cheap internal heuristic, not something another agent needs shared"]]}

blocks.text: A good heuristic is to ask whether another agent or client might reasonably reuse this exact capability tomorrow.
3. Choose the Orchestration Model
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590832-916288211.png
You can build this as one orchestrator that routes to tools directly, or as several specialized sub agents that hand off to each other.
For a support style agent touching three or four systems, a single orchestrator with tool routing is simpler and much easier to observe.
Multi agent handoff earns its complexity when sub tasks need genuinely different reasoning styles, not just different tools.
4. Design the Tool Routing Logic
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590832-168103487.png
The model chooses which tool to call based on the conversation so far and the tool descriptions it was given.
Narrow, clearly described tools route correctly far more often than one giant tool with a mode parameter.
5. Structure Each MCP Server Around One System
Each MCP server should wrap exactly one underlying system, the order database, the knowledge base, the email provider.
Keep each server's tool set narrow and named for the system it fronts, do not let one server quietly grow into three.
6. Manage Context Across Multiple Servers
Raw tool results from three different servers can quickly overwhelm the model's context window.
Each server should return a compact, summarized result, not a full database row or a full document.

blocks.title: Summarize before you return
blocks.content: Have every MCP server trim its own output to what the model actually needs. Pushing that summarization into the server keeps the orchestrator simple and keeps context usage predictable.

blocks.text: 7. Design Permissions and Scoping Per Tool

blocks.alt: Design Permissions and Scoping Per Tool
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590833-211377378.png
Every tool call should carry the caller's identity, and each server should enforce the same authorization the underlying system already has.
Give read only tools like knowledge base search broad access, but scope write tools like sending email far more tightly.

items: Order lookup: read only, scoped to orders tied to the current customer.
Knowledge base search: read only, broadly scoped, low risk.
Send email: write, scoped to a single reply per ticket, never bulk send.

blocks.text: 8. Require Human Approval for Risky Actions

blocks.alt: Require Human Approval for Risky Actions
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590833-308853068.png
Define upfront which actions count as risky, anything that spends money, sends an external message, or deletes data.
Route only those calls through an approval queue, everything else should keep flowing without added friction.

items: Queue the pending action with full context, not just a yes or no prompt.
Set a timeout, and decide what happens if no human responds in time.
Log every approval decision with who approved it and when.

blocks.text: Approval should block only that one action, not the entire conversation the agent is having with the user.
9. Handle Tool Failures and Retries
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590834-287024759.png
Each server should distinguish a validation error the model can fix from a transient outage worth retrying.
If the knowledge base times out mid search, say so explicitly rather than letting the model guess at an incomplete answer.
10. Add Observability From the First Version
Log every tool call across all three servers with caller id, arguments with sensitive fields redacted, latency, and outcome.
A single user turn can span all three servers, so thread one trace id through every call in that turn.
11. Control Cost Per Turn and Per Session
Every model call and every tool call costs money, so cap how many tool calls one turn is allowed to make.
Track cost per session and alert when one user or one tool starts dominating total spend.
12. Think About Latency and Parallel Calls
Independent calls, like an order lookup and a knowledge base search, can run in parallel to cut total latency.
Calls with a real dependency, like sending an email only after approval, must stay sequential.
13. Keep Security Boundaries Between Servers
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441590834-714415394.png
One compromised server credential should never expose the other two systems the agent touches.
Give each server its own scoped credential to its own underlying system, never one shared master key.
14. Test and Evaluate the Whole Agent
Test each MCP server in isolation first, then test full conversations that span all three servers together.
Build a small eval set of realistic customer messages paired with the tool call sequence you expect.
15. Scale the Orchestrator
Keep the orchestrator stateless between turns, and store conversation state in an external store instead.
A stateless orchestrator can run as many instances behind a load balancer with no special coordination.
16. Version Multiple Servers Together
Three servers evolving on their own schedules means schema changes need to stay additive wherever possible.
Pin the agent to known tool schema versions and roll out breaking changes gradually, never all at once.
17. Anticipate Follow-Up Questions
A strong interviewer will push past the first design with harder questions about failure and scale.

items: What happens if the order server and the email server disagree about which ticket this is?
How would this change if a third party, not your own team, ran one of these servers?
What is the blast radius if the email server's credentials leak?
How would you add a fourth tool without breaking the existing three?

blocks.text: Worked Example: A Customer Support Agent
The prompt is design a customer support agent that can look up orders, check a knowledge base, and send email replies.
First, clarify scope. The end user is a paying customer, the agent both reads data and takes the action of sending a reply.
Second, name the three underlying systems, an order management API, a knowledge base search index, and a transactional email provider.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Capability","Type","Notes"],"rows":[["Look up an order by id","MCP server tool","Order Lookup Server, read only, scoped to the current customer"],["Search the knowledge base","MCP server tool","Knowledge Base Server, read only, broad scope"],["Send an email reply","MCP server tool","Email Sender Server, write, gated by human approval"],["Score message urgency","Native function","Cheap internal heuristic, no external system involved"],["Summarize a long order history","Native function","Pure formatting logic before returning context to the model"]]}

blocks.text: Third, pick the orchestration model. One orchestrator routing to three MCP servers plus two native functions is enough here.
Fourth, design routing so order questions hit the order server, policy questions hit the knowledge base, and only a drafted reply hits email.
Fifth, layer in permissions. Order lookups are scoped per customer, knowledge base search is broadly readable, email sending is the one write action.
Sixth, address observability and cost. Every call across all three servers shares one trace id and gets logged with latency and outcome.
Cap this agent at six tool calls per turn, and alert if any single customer session crosses a cost threshold in a day.
That is a complete answer, built in the same order every time, regardless of which three systems the prompt names.
Common Mistakes

items: Turning every capability into an MCP server, including trivial logic that never needed one.
Skipping human approval for actions that spend money or send messages on the user's behalf.
Returning raw tool output straight into context instead of summarizing it first.
Sharing one credential across all three servers instead of scoping each one separately.
Building elaborate multi agent handoffs when a single orchestrator with routing would have worked fine.
Never capping tool calls per turn, so one confused loop can rack up unbounded cost.

blocks.text: Practice
Take the prompt design a multi tool agent for an internal IT helpdesk, and walk through all seventeen steps out loud.

items: Stretch goal one: assume one of the three systems is owned by an external vendor with its own rate limits.
Stretch goal two: add a fourth server and explain how you would version the rollout without breaking the first three.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway
A multi tool agent design question rewards the same discipline as designing a single MCP server, just applied across several systems at once.
Clarify scope, sort capabilities into servers versus native functions, design routing and permissions, then gate risky actions behind a human.
